attacks.claim: S2's escalation-alert spec is internally inconsistent, so its own verification case (h) cannot be implemented unambiguously: 'cooldown doubling per failure past the free allowance' plus 'alert at most once per escalation' implies one alert per post-allowance failure — 12 raw recordFailure calls with freeAttempts=5 yields 7 escalations, yet test (h) demands 'exactly 3 non-null alerts across 12 failures'. An implementer must invent either a different definition of 'escalation' or an unstated call sequence (interleaved allow()/clock advances) to make the numbers meet, and two implementers will invent different ones.
attacks.evidence: opus.json S2 intent ('doubling per failure past the free allowance', 'ONLY on crossing into cooldown and then at most once per escalation') vs S2 verification (h) ('assert exactly 3 non-null alerts across 12 failures'). No sequence of 12 bare recordFailure calls under the stated policy produces 3 escalations: failures 6..12 each either double the cooldown (7 alerts) or are all inside one cooldown (1 alert). Neither reading gives 3.
attacks.repair: Define 'escalation' operationally in S2 — e.g. an alert fires when a bucket transitions from allowed to cooling (recordFailure while allow(key).ok is true and the new failure count exceeds freeAttempts) — and rewrite test (h) as an explicit scripted sequence of allow/recordFailure/clock-advance calls with the expected alert positions, so the count follows from the script rather than from a guessed semantics.

attacks.claim: The blast radius omits apps/desktop: src-tauri/lib.rs states the contract 'The server accepts ANY non-empty LEDRUMS_PIN' twice (doc comment on parse_pin and a Rust test named parses_non_numeric_pin_matching_server_behavior), and S1's boot-time minimum makes both statements false. S6 claims to update documentation 'where operators actually read them' but names only the pin-gate.ts header, leaving a cross-language docs-truth breach that will mislead the next person touching the desktop banner parser.
attacks.evidence: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:242 ('The server accepts ANY non-empty `LEDRUMS_PIN`, so the token is captured up to the next whitespace or `)`') and lib.rs:674 (test comment repeating the claim). opus.json S6 files list contains only apps/server/src/pin-gate.ts and the probe artifact; interface_deltas and every step's files field name no apps/desktop path.
attacks.repair: Add the two lib.rs comment sites to S6's file list (comment-only edit: 'accepts any LEDRUMS_PIN of at least MIN_PIN_LENGTH characters; charset still unconstrained, so the parser must not assume digits'). No Rust behaviour change — the parser and its non-numeric test remain correct.

attacks.claim: The global tier is an attacker-operable denial-of-service switch against the legitimate remote drummer, and the plan never names this availability regression: 100 failed handshakes per 60s (trivial for one attacker via the tunnel) put EVERY non-trusted peer into a renewable maxMs cooldown, so the drummer's remote phone — which today can always connect with the right PIN — can be locked out indefinitely for the cost of ~2 requests/second. known_gaps discusses the global tier only as 'efficacy against a distributed guess'; the induced-lockout cost of that same tier appears nowhere.
attacks.evidence: opus.json S2 intent: 'a GLOBAL tier of globalFailures = 100 inside windowMs that applies one shared maxMs cooldown to every non-trusted peer'; behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.known_gaps third gap discusses only parameter judgement, not legitimate-user lockout; open question 1 covers messaging of the 4401, not availability. Trading PIN-compromise for attacker-controlled denial is a defensible design, but it is a product-visible regression that must be stated, not implied.
attacks.repair: State the trade-off explicitly in S2's intent and known_gaps ('an active attacker can hold remote access closed; the monitor alert with scope global is the operator's signal'), and consider exempting peers with a recorded prior success in the current run from the global tier — recordSuccess already exists to carry that bit.

attacks.claim: The final wave pairs S5 and S6 concurrently but both list docs/plans/2026-07-26-deep-review/artifacts/pin-throttle-probe.json in their files — the wave is not file-disjoint, so two implementers running the stated schedule write the same artifact.
attacks.evidence: opus.json sequencing [["S1","S2"],["S3"],["S4"],["S5","S6"]]; S5 files includes docs/plans/2026-07-26-deep-review/artifacts/pin-throttle-probe.json and S6 files lists the same path.
attacks.repair: Drop the artifact path from S6's files (S6 only references the probe output, it does not produce it), or serialize S6 after S5.

attacks.claim: S5's before-state run ('Run the same script against baseline sha 3708648') is not executable as written: the probe script does not exist at the baseline sha, and the plan never says how a baseline server is obtained (separate worktree, separate build, which port/env) on a repo whose working branch has all six steps landed. An implementer either invents a worktree procedure or silently skips the baseline run and the parity artifact loses its 'before' half.
attacks.evidence: opus.json S5 verification: 'Run the same script against baseline sha 3708648 to capture the before-state'; scripts/pin-throttle-probe.mjs is created by S5 itself, so it is absent at 3708648, and no step describes checking out or building the baseline server.
attacks.repair: Specify the mechanism in S5: `git worktree add <scratch> 3708648`, build there, boot that server, run the HEAD copy of the probe against its port; record both runs' shas inside the JSON artifact.

attacks.claim: peerKeyFrom's declared signature accepts headers as Record<string, string | string[] | undefined> but the spec only defines behaviour for the string case ('returns cf:<cf-connecting-ip>'); when Node surfaces a repeated header as string[] — or when isViaCloudflare is true via cdn-loop alone with cf-connecting-ip absent — the key is unspecified, and a naive template interpolation yields 'cf:1.2.3.4,5.6.7.8' or 'cf:undefined', silently merging distinct peers into one bucket.
attacks.evidence: opus.json S2 intent signature: 'peerKeyFrom(remoteAddress: string | null | undefined, headers: Record<string, string | string[] | undefined>)'; apps/server/src/pin-gate.ts:111-115 shows isViaCloudflare returns true when EITHER cf-connecting-ip OR cdn-loop is present, so the cloudflare-but-no-cf-connecting-ip branch is reachable.
attacks.repair: Specify: array header → first element; via-cloudflare with absent/empty cf-connecting-ip → fall through to ip:<remoteAddress>; add both as cases in admission-throttle.test.ts.

attacks.claim: Changing admitDecision's third parameter from a positional boolean to an options object breaks consumers the plan never names — any call site passing `true`/`false` outside main.ts and pin-gate.test.ts would silently coerce or fail.
attacks.evidence: Grep of apps/server/src at HEAD: admitDecision is called only at apps/server/src/main.ts:486 and in apps/server/src/pin-gate.test.ts (cases at lines 52-75) — exactly the two sites the plan names. A boolean third argument would also be a type error against AdmitContext, so `pnpm typecheck` catches any missed site rather than coercing.
attacks.plan_response: behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.checks[1]: 'pnpm typecheck — proves the admitDecision signature change has exactly the call sites the plan names (main.ts:486 and pin-gate.test.ts) and no silent boolean-to-object coercion elsewhere.' My independent grep confirms the named call-site set is complete.

attacks.claim: Reusing close code 4401 for throttled refusals makes the web client's PIN overlay tell a cooling-down drummer 'incorrect PIN' when their PIN is correct, and pauses its reconnect loop (apps/web/src/lib/ws/client.ts:205-208) — a UX lie the plan ships knowingly.
attacks.evidence: apps/web/src/lib/ws/client.ts:205-208 pauses reconnect on WS_CLOSE_INVALID_PIN; a throttled correct-PIN attempt closes with the same code.
attacks.plan_response: The summary states the trade explicitly ('the cost is that a throttled legitimate user sees incorrect PIN... recorded as an open question rather than silently widened into a UI initiative') and open_questions[0] escalates the 4429-vs-4401 decision to Trent with blocks_execution:false. The cost is named, bounded, and routed to the owner — that is an answered attack, not a hole.

attacks.claim: S1's boot-time throw on a sub-4-character LEDRUMS_PIN turns a today-working configuration into a server that refuses to start — including under the desktop sidecar and scripts/dev.mjs, where the failure surfaces as an opaque dead process rather than a clear message.
attacks.evidence: apps/server/src/main.ts:86 calls resolvePin at module top level; apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:375-394 spawns the server inheriting the user environment, so an inherited short LEDRUMS_PIN kills the sidecar at boot.
attacks.plan_response: S1 intent argues fail-closed over silent-drop ('a silently-dropped PIN means an OPEN server') and rollback_strategy names this as 'the single operator-visible irreversibility... a server configured with a sub-4-character LEDRUMS_PIN will refuse to boot — the fix is to set a longer PIN, and it must be called out in the release note.' The throw message text is specified in S1, so the failure is not opaque in the server log.

attacks.claim: The constant-time property of credentialsEqual is asserted but no test can prove it, so the primitive-obsession finding's core security claim rests on unverifiable evidence.
attacks.evidence: Timing assertions in vitest are inherently flaky; nothing in pin-gate.test.ts can measure comparison timing reliably.
attacks.plan_response: known_gaps second gap concedes exactly this and substitutes structural evidence: 'both credentials provably route through the single timingSafeEqual call site; grep must show zero remaining `=== pin` comparisons in pin-gate.ts'. That is the strongest evidence available for this property and it is falsifiable by a command.

required_repairs: S2: define 'escalation' operationally and rewrite verification (h) as an explicit scripted call sequence whose expected alert count follows from the definition — the current spec and test count contradict each other.
S2: specify peerKeyFrom for string[] headers and for via-cloudflare requests lacking cf-connecting-ip (fall through to ip:<remoteAddress>), with test cases for both.

S2/known_gaps: state the global-tier trade-off — an active attacker can hold remote access closed at ~2 req/s — and either accept it explicitly or exempt previously-succeeded peers from the global cooldown.
S6: remove the pin-throttle-probe.json artifact from S6's files (or serialize S6 after S5) so the final wave is file-disjoint.
S5: specify the baseline-run mechanism (git worktree at 3708648, build there, run the HEAD probe script against that server) so the before-state half of the parity artifact is actually producible.
S6: extend the docs pass to apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/lib.rs:242 and :674, whose comments assert the now-false 'accepts ANY non-empty LEDRUMS_PIN' contract.
